lit.\u0027\u003cp\u003eEl \u003cb\u003eespec:
"

The absorption spectrum is A versus λ. Work is done at λmax because there ε is maximal (more sensitivity) and the error from a small shift in λ is minimal. The color of the solution is the complement of the light it absorbs: KMnO₄ absorbs ~525 nm (green) and looks violet.

"
lit.\u0027\u003cp\u003eLa \u003cb\u003eley d:
"

The Beer–Lambert law states A = ε·b·c: ε is the molar absorptivity (L mol⁻¹ cm⁻¹), b the path length (cm) and c the concentration (mol/L). Doubling c or b doubles A. It is valid for dilute solutions; at A > 1.5–2 deviations appear due to stray light and the detector loses precision (turn on “Stray light”).

"
lit.\u0027\u003cp\u003eSe mide la A de la \u:
"

The A of the unknown sample is measured and interpolated on the line: c = (A − n)/m. Never extrapolate beyond the range of the standards. Compare your result with the real concentration (hidden until this step) and calculate the relative error.

"
lit.\u0027\u003cp\u003eSe preparan \u003cb\u:
"

Standards of known concentration are prepared and their A is measured at λmax. A linear regression is made: the slope m = ε·b. The coefficient of determination R² (≥ 0.999 is excellent) indicates how linear the response is. The standards must span the range of the sample.

"
lit.\u0027\u003cp\u003eUn \u003cb\u003eespec:
"

A spectrophotometer sends monochromatic light of intensity I₀ through a cuvette; the detector measures the transmitted light I. The transmittance is T = I/I₀ and the absorbance A = −log₁₀T. T = 100 % ↔ A = 0; T = 10 % ↔ A = 1; T = 1 % ↔ A = 2. The blank (solvent) is measured first to set A = 0.

"
